title: Epoxy Resin Flooring｜Self-Levelling, Anti-Static, Water-Based Systems｜Huiying
desc: Six epoxy flooring systems: thin-build, self-levelling, clear, anti-static, water-based and structural repair, over a shared primer and body coat.
kw: epoxy flooring, epoxy resin floor, self-levelling flooring, anti-static flooring, cleanroom flooring, industrial floor coating
lead: Six systems over a primer and body coat common to every build-up — specified against the mechanical strength, chemical resistance and cleanliness the facility actually requires.
intro: **A floor is a structure, not a coat of paint.** A complete epoxy floor is built in three stages: the **primer** penetrates and seals the substrate and determines whether the system stays down; the **body coat** is the structural layer, providing thickness, flatness and mechanical strength, and it is where overall cost is controlled; the **topcoat** determines appearance, abrasion and chemical resistance, and how easily the floor can be cleaned. Omit any one layer and the other two cannot perform.
series_p: Primer and body coat are base layers common to every build-up and are not counted as systems; the six systems that follow are selected or combined according to requirement.
cta_p: Send us the facility type, area, pattern of use and available downtime, and we will return a suitable system and material specification.

series.name: Primer (base layer)
series.tag: Common to all systems · substrate penetration and sealing
series.desc: An epoxy primer penetrates the concrete substrate, bonds tightly to the base layer and seals the capillary structure, raising the adhesion of the whole floor. Once the substrate is prepared, the primer is roller-applied across the full area before the body coat and topcoat. Solvent-based and solvent-free grades are available according to substrate condition, with a dedicated formulation for low temperatures.
feat: Penetrates and seals capillaries, preventing blistering in the layers above
Substantially improves adhesion of the system to the base
General and low-temperature grades available
High-adhesion grades suit difficult or aged substrates
series.use: All cementitious substrates; sealing prior to refurbishment of an existing floor

spec.v: First layer, before the body coat

series.name: Body coat (base layer)
series.tag: Common to all systems · structural layer
series.desc: The body coat is the structural core of the floor, providing thickness, flatness, mechanical strength and impact resistance. It can be applied in stages to build 1–3 mm, or as a high-filler grade for greater thickness above 4 mm. It is also where overall cost is controlled — thickness is established here rather than by stacking expensive topcoat material.
feat: Improves flatness, thickness and mechanical strength
Raises impact and abrasion resistance
Reduces overall material cost
Colour can be matched close to the topcoat so local wear is less visible
series.use: Factories, warehousing and car parks where loading and impact resistance matter

spec.v: 1–3 mm applied in stages; 4 mm and above with high-filler grades
After the primer, before the topcoat

series.name: Thin-build topcoat systems
series.desc: Thin-build topcoats are straightforward to apply, give a smooth attractive finish, offer a wide colour choice and are reasonably priced, making them the most widely used finish. They effectively prevent dusting and suit facilities that want a good appearance without cleanroom standards. Normally roller-applied; on large areas, pot life and labour allocation need planning.
feat: Easy to apply with a short programme
Wide colour choice; areas can be colour-coded
Prevents dusting and improves the working environment
Good abrasion resistance for frequent vehicle and foot traffic
series.use: Car parks, general factories, garages, warehousing

spec.v: Thin film; the most economical in cost and programme

series.name: Self-levelling systems
series.desc: Self-levelling systems offer excellent adhesion and surface smoothness, high gloss and good water and chemical resistance, forming a seamless monolithic finish. The material must be trowelled evenly in a single operation, with strict control of pot life and labour allocation; large areas must be zoned and planned in advance.
feat: Smooth and seamless, reducing contaminant adhesion
High gloss and good visual quality
Good water and chemical resistance
Easy to clean; suits facilities with high cleanliness requirements
series.use: Hospitals, pharmaceutical and electronics plants, food factories, cleanrooms, schools, offices

series.name: Clear topcoat systems
series.desc: A clear topcoat forms a protective layer over the floor with high gloss, transparency, strength and acid and alkali resistance. It does not alter the appearance beneath, so it suits spaces where the existing floor character is to be retained while adding protection — commonly over terrazzo and decorative floors.
feat: High gloss and transparency; original appearance unchanged
High strength with acid and alkali resistance
Protective layer for decorative floors
Solvent-free grades available
series.use: Hotels, residential, design studios, offices, pharmaceutical and food facilities; terrazzo and display spaces

series.name: Anti-static systems
series.desc: An anti-static floor dissipates static charge accumulating at the surface, preventing sparking. The system comprises a conductive primer, anti-static body coat and anti-static topcoat, installed together with an earthed copper foil grid to form a complete conductive path. The materials also provide the gloss, impact, chemical and abrasion performance of a conventional floor.
feat: Dissipates surface static charge and prevents sparking
Requires an earthed copper foil grid to complete the path
Combines gloss, impact and chemical resistance
Trowel or spray grades available
series.use: Semiconductor and electronics plants, server rooms, hazardous areas, instrument facilities

spec.v: Conductive primer + anti-static body coat + anti-static topcoat + earthed copper grid

series.name: Water-based systems
series.desc: Water-based epoxy flooring is designed as an environmentally responsible option: no VOC, low odour, good appearance and sound cure characteristics. Water-based epoxy is more sensitive to temperature and humidity, so ventilation must be confirmed; application below 10°C is not recommended as it compromises the cure. Mixing must be by powered stirrer and the material used within its pot life.
feat: No VOC and low odour; suits facilities that cannot close for long
Good appearance and cure characteristics
Better tolerance of damp conditions
First choice for basements and poorly ventilated spaces
series.use: Food, electronics, pharmaceutical, cosmetics and paper plants; underground car parks and other ventilation-limited spaces

spec.v: Confirm adequate ventilation in the work area

series.name: Structural repair products
series.desc: Substrate defects must be resolved before flooring is applied. This range covers repair and strengthening materials for cracks, spalling, honeycombing and areas of insufficient local strength. Applying a floor over unresolved substrate defects is one of the most common causes of failure.
feat: Treats cracks, spalling and honeycombing
Strengthens areas of insufficient local strength
Essential preparation before the flooring system
series.use: Refurbishment works; substrate preparation before floor renewal

spec.v: Before the flooring system is applied

faq.q: What is the difference between epoxy and PU flooring?
faq.a: Epoxy offers better hardness, abrasion resistance and chemical resistance, but lower flexibility and less ability to bridge substrate movement than PU. PU floors are more elastic and tolerate thermal movement better, suiting facilities with temperature variation or requiring some resilience, such as cold stores and food plant washdown areas. General factories, car parks and cleanrooms are predominantly epoxy.

faq.q: What condition does the substrate need to be in?
faq.a: Three factors: moisture content, flatness and strength. Epoxy is highly sensitive to moisture, and an over-wet substrate leads to blistering and delamination. Dusting surfaces, oil contamination or failed coatings must be ground off or removed. Areas of low strength, cracking or honeycombing should be made good with repair materials first. This preparation takes a significant share of the programme, and cannot be skipped.

faq.q: How thick should the floor be?
faq.a: It depends on loading and use. Light office use is served by a thin-build topcoat; factories with forklifts, racking or heavy vehicles need body coat thickness as the priority, built up to 1–3 mm in stages or above 4 mm with high-filler grades. Insufficient thickness leads to crushing or delamination at load points.

faq.q: How long does the facility need to close?
faq.a: It depends on the system and area. Thin-build systems have the shortest programme; self-levelling and anti-static systems involve more layers, each requiring cure time, so take longer. In practice work is usually phased so the facility can remain partly operational. Cure times must be built into the programme — compressing intervals to save time is a frequent cause of failure.

faq.q: Our underground car park is poorly ventilated. Is there a suitable material?
faq.a: Yes. Water-based epoxy systems have no VOC and low odour, making them the first choice for ventilation-limited spaces. Note that water-based epoxy is more sensitive to temperature and humidity; application below 10°C is not recommended, and ventilation should still be confirmed during installation.

faq.q: Do food plants have particular requirements?
faq.a: Food plants are among the most demanding environments, combining hot washdown, fats, organic acids and frequent cleaning. Thermal and chemical resistance specifications should be confirmed explicitly, and a seamless self-levelling system is preferred to reduce contaminant adhesion. Falls to drainage and detailing around gullies should be planned at the same time.
